strengths: Proposes a genuinely novel and well-motivated Interactive UI-to-Code paradigm that reframes UI coding as iterative generation, polishing, and editing driven by rendering feedback, and connects this to test-time scaling in a principled way.

The three-stage training pipeline (continual pretraining on noisy real web data, SFT on curated data, RL with a designed verifier) is a substantial systems contribution, and the paper presents a fairly complete recipe rather than a single trick.

The reward design is thoughtfully engineered and ablated: the progression from vanilla verifier scoring to comparator scoring to round-robin ranking (Algorithms 1-3) is clearly described and empirically justified, and the finding that a weak verifier (un-tuned GLM-4.5V) can degrade RL is a useful insight.

Evaluation is broad (Design2Code, Flame-React-Eval, Web2Code, plus the curated UI2Code-Real and UIPolish-bench), and all baselines are re-evaluated under a single consistent protocol, which is better practice than mixing published numbers.

Empirical results are strong and internally consistent with the paradigm: the model surpasses leading closed-source systems (Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro) on several benchmarks, and the test-time scaling curve shows monotonic gains on real data up to N=5 (~12% improvement).
The ablations on real-world data in RL (Table 4) and on reward choice (Table 3b) provide actionable takeaways for the community.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim rests almost entirely on VLM-judge metrics (o4-mini for UI-to-code, Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing) rather than the standard Design2Code metrics (CLIP similarity, block-match, element-level matching) used by prior work. Without reporting standard metrics, direct comparison to the established literature is difficult, and the reliability of a single VLM judge with an arbitrary pass threshold (score >= 80) is not validated (e.g., no human agreement study).

Potential evaluator/verifier family bias: the model is initialized from GLM-4.1V-9B-Base and the RL reward verifier is a fine-tuned GLM-4.5V, i.e., the same model family is used to both generate and (via RL) optimize toward its own judgments. The paper does not analyze or rule out correlated bias between the reward model and the trained policy.

Inconsistent baseline numbers across tables undermine confidence: UI2CodeN-SFT scores 79.3 on Design2Code in Table 1, but 72.3 in Table 3b and 81.5 in Table 4. Even if these come from different ablation runs (batch size 32 vs 64, lr 1e-6 vs default), the paper does not clearly explain the discrepancies, making the reported gains hard to attribute.

The RL-with-CLIP-reward result degrades substantially below the SFT baseline (62.0 vs 72.3 on Design2Code, 72.2 vs 85.0 on Flame). A ~10-point drop is unusually large and is attributed only to 'visual similarity is insufficient'; the possibility of reward hacking, instability, or a flawed CLIP-reward implementation is not investigated, which weakens the reward-design argument.

The curated benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench) and the polishing success criterion (C>B, with an asserted 50% 'genuine capability' threshold) are self-defined and somewhat arbitrary. No inter-annotator or inter-judge agreement is reported, and fairness of these self-constructed sets across competing models is asserted rather than demonstrated.

No experimental comparison against prior UI-to-code methods/systems discussed in related work (e.g., ScreenCoder, DCGen, WebSight, Pix2code, WebCode2M). The related-work section promises agent-based comparisons but the experiments only compare generic VLMs.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract claims 'code and models are available at' but provides no URL/link, and key details (exact data sources and filtering thresholds for the ~10M crawled pairs, full RL/SFT hyperparameters, verifier fine-tuning data) are only partially specified.

Presentation issues: Table 1 places the paper's own UI2CodeN-9B-SFT and UI2CodeN-9B-RL rows under the 'Closed-source VLM' section, which is misleading, and several claims ('first open-source VLM to incorporate...', 'first to present the full training recipe') are unverifiable as stated.

strengths: The interactive UI-to-code paradigm is well motivated: the argument that pixel-level fidelity cannot be verified without rendering (font fallback, browser defaults, DPI) is concrete and correctly identifies a real limitation of single-turn generation.

The three-stage recipe (continual pretraining on noisy crawled web data, SFT on curated/synthetic data, RL on unpaired screenshots) is a sensible way to trade off data realism and code cleanliness, and the description is detailed enough to be informative.

The reward design in Appendix A.1 is the most substantive technical contribution: the progression from independent verifier scoring to a calibrated comparator to round-robin pairwise ranking addresses a genuine problem (calibration drift and fairness across N rollouts), and Table 3a shows a monotone improvement.

All baselines are re-evaluated under one protocol rather than copying numbers from prior papers, which is the right instinct, and the model/code release statement suggests an intent toward reproducibility.
The test-time scaling experiment (Table 2) demonstrates a plausible cost/quality trade-off that is a useful direction for the community.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claims rest on a non-standard metric. The paper reports 'state of the art' on Design2Code, Flame-React-Eval and Web2Code, but evaluates with a VLM score thresholded at 80 (Eq. 3) rather than the benchmarks' own protocols (CLIP + element matching for Design2Code, DINOv2 similarity for Flame). These numbers are therefore not comparable to any published result, and no standard metric is reported, so the headline claims are not verifiable.

The evaluator is a conflict of interest: o4-mini is used as the UI-to-code judge (Appendix A.3.1) while also appearing as a compared baseline in Table 1. Similarly, Gemini-2.5-Pro is the UI-polishing judge (Appendix A.3.2) while also being a competitor whose polishing numbers (74/68) are compared against. Worse, the RL reward is itself a VLM similarity score (GLM-4.5V), i.e., the evaluation is of the same form as the training objective, creating an obvious circularity/verifier-exploitation risk that is never analyzed.

Internal numerical inconsistencies undermine trust. Table 3b lists the UI2CodeN-SFT baseline at 72.3 on Design2Code, whereas Table 1 reports UI2CodeN-9B-SFT at 79.3. Table 3a reports the round-robin RL at 93/79 (avg 86.0) while Table 1 reports 94/80 for the final RL model. These gaps are never explained, and no variance or seed information is given anywhere.

A headline capability is not evaluated at all. UI editing is claimed as one of three core capabilities and in the contributions list, but it appears only as qualitative demo images in Appendix A.5.2, with no benchmark, no metric, and no comparison. The claim 'first open-source VLM to incorporate UI-to-code, UI polishing and UI editing' is thus partly unsubstantiated.

The staged training is not ablated. Despite the claim of presenting 'the first full training recipe,' there is no ablation isolating the effect of the 20M-sample continual pretraining or the SFT data construction. Since the model is initialized from GLM-4.1V-9B-Base and GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking is itself the strongest open baseline (64.7 on Design2Code), it is impossible to tell how much of the gain comes from the proposed recipe versus the base model and scale of crawled data.

Novelty is overstated. Iterative self-refinement with rendered feedback (self-revision/self-refine style loops) is a well-known idea and was already explored for this exact task; the paper neither cites nor compares against such self-revision baselines, so it cannot show that its interactive polishing is better than simply re-prompting other models. The 'new paradigm' framing is not supported by a distinguishing experiment.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract states 'Our code and models are available at' with no URL, the 10M crawled pairs and 80K SFT samples are not described in reproducible detail, the verifier fine-tuning (data, size, procedure) is omitted, and the RL data (12K Mind2Web + 30K synthetic, plus 'earlier UI2CodeN runs') is not released or specified precisely enough to re-run.

There is no limitations section, no error analysis, and no research-ethics discussion. Crawling ~10M webpages and training on their HTML/screenshots raises copyright/licensing and ToS questions that are not addressed. Benchmark sizes (115 real pages; 100+100 polishing) are small with no significance testing, and the UI2Code-Synthetic benchmark used in Table 2 is never defined in Appendix A.4.

Several baseline numbers look implausible and are left unexplained (e.g., GPT-4o 35.3 on Design2Code vs 75.0 on Flame; Gemini-2.5-flash 17/24 on polishing vs Gemini-2.5-pro 74/68). This pattern suggests the metric is dominated by rendering/formatting artifacts rather than polishing or coding ability, which would invalidate the '50% threshold' argument used to claim that open-source VLMs lack polishing ability.

strengths: Tackles an important and practically relevant problem, UI-to-code generation, with an interactive paradigm that mirrors real front-end development and enables test-time scaling through iterative polishing.

Introduces a well-motivated three-stage training pipeline: continual pretraining on large-scale noisy real webpages, SFT on curated synthetic data, and RL with a VLM-based verifier. This directly addresses the trade-off between data scale/noise and code quality.

Reports strong empirical results: UI2CodeN-9B-RL achieves 88.6 on Design2Code, 95.0 on Flame, 92.5 on Web2Code, and 76.5 on UI2Code-Real, outperforming much larger open-source VLMs and rivaling several leading closed-source models. UI polishing results (80.0 real, 94.0 synthetic) are also competitive.

Proposes a thoughtful RL reward design using comparator scoring and round-robin ranking; ablations show VLM-based rewards outperform CLIP rewards and that adding real webpages in RL improves real-world performance.
Demonstrates test-time scaling via recursive UI polishing, with gains across interaction rounds on both real and synthetic benchmarks.
Provides substantial implementation detail in the appendix, including reward algorithms and evaluation prompts, which helps clarify the method.
The open-source release of code/models and the full training recipe, if delivered, would be valuable to the community.
weaknesses: UI editing is claimed as one of the three key unified capabilities, but it is evaluated only with qualitative demo cases in the appendix; there is no quantitative benchmark or metric for editing, so the claim that the model incorporates robust UI editing is not empirically supported.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies across tables. Table 1 reports UI2CodeN-9B-RL at 76.5 on UI2Code-Real, while Table 2 reports N=1 at 66.0 and N=5 at only 74.0 on the same benchmark, making the test-time scaling result appear weaker than the single-turn RL model. Similarly, Table 3b reports SFT at 72.3 on Design2Code while Table 1 reports SFT at 79.3, which undermines the RL reward ablation.

Evaluation relies heavily on VLM judges (o4-mini for UI-to-code and Gemini-2.5-Pro for UI polishing) with an arbitrary success threshold (score >= 80), without human validation, inter-judge agreement, or comparison to the original benchmark metrics such as CLIP and element matching. Using Gemini-2.5-Pro as an evaluator while also comparing it as a model raises potential bias concerns.

The test-time scaling claim is weakened because the scaling curve appears to start from a lower-performing checkpoint (likely SFT) rather than the final RL model; the paper does not show whether polishing improves the final RL model beyond its already strong single-turn result.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript says code and models are available at a blank URL, no dataset release details or compute budget are given, the initialization from an 'early checkpoint' of GLM-4.1V-9B-Base may not be publicly accessible, and the fine-tuning of the GLM-4.5V verifier is not fully specified.

No limitations, broader-impact, or ethics discussion is provided. This is especially relevant because the work crawls and renders real webpages, generates code from screenshots, and could raise copyright, licensing, privacy, and environmental-cost concerns.

Potential data contamination is not analyzed. The pretraining corpus uses Common Crawl and large-scale crawling, and the RL data includes Mind2Web and synthetic examples; overlap with Design2Code, Web2Code, Flame, or the newly proposed real-world benchmarks is not discussed.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not discuss failure modes of UI polishing or reward hacking, despite using a VLM as a reward model and noting that weak rewards can misdirect RL.

Presentation issues remain: duplicated references for ScreenCoder (Jiang et al., 2025a/2025b), typos such as 'Sj > S', missing superscripts in UI2CodeN, and confusing table grouping where the proposed models appear after the closed-source block.

strengths: The paper tackles a practical and timely problem (UI-to-code) and proposes an interactive visual optimization framework that unifies drafting, polishing, and editing as a closed-loop process.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering multiple benchmarks and including new real-world and polishing benchmarks, with human evaluation on challenging subsets.

The three-stage training pipeline (continual pre-training, SFT, RL) is described with reasonable detail, and the paper includes useful analyses such as reward hacking checks, evaluator stability, and human-VLM alignment.
The proposed tournament-based relative reward is a plausible heuristic that, in the authors' experiments, outperforms absolute reward and CLIP-based reward for UI polishing and drafting.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification for RVPO is flawed: the rank-based surrogate objective in Eq. (7) is constant (0.5) for any policy under a symmetric pairwise preference model, so it provides no learning signal. The paper does not derive the actual objective optimized by the tournament reward plus GRPO, leaving the core method unsupported.
The reward construction in Algorithm 1 still compares absolute scores (S_i > S_j) from a VLM verifier, contradicting the claim that RVPO eliminates reliance on calibrated absolute scores.

Reported results are inconsistent: Table 1 lists UI2Code-Real at 76.5 and UIPolish-Synthetic at 94.0, while Table 3 reports UI2Code-Real at 74.0 (N=5) and UI2Code-Synthetic at 97.0 (N=3). This discrepancy undermines the claimed test-time scaling.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance is overstated: on Design2Code, Web2Code, and UIPolish-Real, GPT-5/Gemini-2.5-Pro/Claude-4.5 outperform or match UI2Code, so the assertion that it consistently outperforms larger models is not supported.

Reproducibility is limited: despite claiming an open-source 9B model, no code, model weights, training data, or the fine-tuned reward verifier are provided, and key components (e.g., verifier SFT with Gemini-2.5-Pro teacher) are not fully reproducible.

The main evaluation relies heavily on VLM judges (o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro) with an arbitrary score threshold of 80; human validation is only on small subsets, and no comparison to simple group-sampling baselines (e.g., best-of-N or rejection-sampling fine-tuning) is provided to isolate the benefit of RVPO.
The iterative refinement claim is not consistently supported: Table 16 shows polishing accuracy decreasing across rounds (66.0 → 64.7 → 63.3 → 65.8), yet the text claims consistent improvement.
Minor presentation issues: inconsistent acronym (RVPO vs. VRPO), unclear benchmark naming (UI2Code-Real vs. UI2Code-Synthetic), and some tables lack clear definitions.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem, UI-to-code generation, and gives a coherent high-level motivation for treating it as an interactive, feedback-driven optimization process rather than a single-pass generation task.

The proposed three-stage pipeline (continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with rendered visual feedback) is a substantial engineering effort, and the resulting 9B model is competitive with much larger models on several reported benchmarks.

The appendices are unusually detailed, including reward-verifier prompts, verifier fine-tuning details, human-evaluation protocols, variance analysis, reward-hacking checks, and efficiency breakdowns.

The relative/tournament-based reward design is intuitively appealing, and the ablation on UI polishing (Figure 3(a)) provides some evidence that relative visual preference rewards outperform an absolute verifier for that task.
The paper includes human evaluation on Design2Code-HARD and UIEdit-Bench, and attempts to validate VLM judges against human judgments, which is a positive step for this domain.
Ethical considerations around web-scale data collection, PII filtering, copyright, licensing, and benchmark decontamination are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is overstated. Table 1 shows GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro outperform UI2CodeN-RL on Design2Code and UIPolish-Real, and Table 2 shows GPT-5 is better on all CLIP/component metrics. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless claim state-of-the-art performance across UI drafting, polishing, and editing, which is not supported by the reported numbers.

The main UI-polishing evaluation uses Gemini-2.5-Pro as the judge, while Appendix A.2 states that the visual comparator/reward verifier is supervised-fine-tuned on Gemini-2.5-Pro annotations. This is a direct train/test evaluator overlap and raises serious concerns that polishing results are inflated by optimizing toward the same judge used for evaluation. No human evaluation on UIPolish-bench is provided to rule this out.

The method description is internally inconsistent. The acronym alternates between RVPO and VRPO. More importantly, Appendix A.1 describes the UI-drafting reward as an absolute normalized GLM-4.5V score, which conflicts with Algorithm 1 and the paper-wide claim that RVPO optimizes relative visual rankings for both drafting and polishing.

The UI-drafting ablation does not actually compare RVPO against absolute VLM rewards. Figure 3(b) shows only SFT, CLIP reward, and VLM reward, yet the text claims the VLM absolute reward 'still underperforms relative to RVPO' without showing an RVPO condition. This leaves a central claim about RVPO for drafting unsupported.

The test-time scaling claim is only partially supported. Table 3 shows improvement on UI2Code-Real and UI2Code-Synthetic, but Appendix Table 16 reports polishing accuracies of 66.0, 64.7, 63.3, and 65.8 across rounds, i.e. fluctuation rather than consistent improvement. The appendix also incorrectly references 'Table 2 of the main paper' when discussing polishing trends.

Reproducibility is weak. There is no code/model/data link, the newly proposed benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench) are not released, the judge fine-tuning triplet data are not released, exact RL data composition and sample counts are unclear, and compute requirements are not reported.

The new benchmarks are small and under-specified: UI2Code-Real has 115 samples, and UIPolish-bench has 100 synthetic + 100 real samples. Annotation protocols, inter-annotator agreement, sampling criteria, and licensing details are limited, making them weak bases for SOTA claims.

Human evaluation is limited. Design2Code-HARD uses only 80 samples and two annotators without inter-annotator agreement or significance testing; UIEdit-Bench has 69 tasks; and there is no human evaluation of the main UI-polishing task, despite polishing being a central contribution.

The theoretical objective in Eq. (7) is questionable. Maximizing expected pairwise preference among samples from the same policy can be degenerate or exploitable through judge bias, and no formal analysis is given to show that it reliably drives the policy toward the target UI. Removing KL regularization without training-stability curves or mode-collapse analysis compounds this concern.

Reward-hacking analysis is too narrow. It checks only the ratio of absolute positioning, but does not analyze style bias, judge-specific artifacts, overfitting to Gemini preferences, or other shortcuts that a VLM judge may reward.

There is no dedicated limitations section. The paper claims model-agnostic applicability to broader executable generation problems, but only instantiates the approach on one 9B UI model and does not discuss failure modes, compute cost, or dependence on the visual judge.

Presentation has multiple issues: inconsistent acronyms, inconsistent model naming (UI2Code^N vs UI2Code-N), incorrect table references, and several claims in the abstract/conclusion that are stronger than the evidence in the tables.

strengths: Reformulates UI-to-code as interactive visual optimization, a clear and practically motivated paradigm that matches iterative UI development and enables test-time scaling via rendered feedback.
Introduces RVPO with tournament-based relative visual rewards, a well-motivated way to avoid unstable absolute VLM scores and integrate preference signals into GRPO.
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple UI-to-code and polishing/editing benchmarks, including real-world and synthetic settings, with comparisons to strong open- and closed-source models.

Strong empirical results: a 9B model achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models and is competitive with or outperforms much larger closed-source systems on several tasks, especially UI polishing and editing.
Includes human evaluations on Design2Code-HARD and UIEdit-Bench plus human-VLM alignment and variance analyses, which strengthen confidence in the reported gains.
Extensive appendices provide reward verifier details, prompts, training configurations, reward-hacking checks, efficiency analysis, and ethical/data-handling discussion.
Addresses an important and timely problem with potential impact on front-end development and UI automation.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated: no explicit artifact/code/model link is provided, training uses large-scale data and proprietary teacher annotations, and the model is described as open-source despite a research-only non-commercial release.

UI polishing evaluation relies on Gemini-2.5-Pro as the judge while the reward verifier is trained to imitate Gemini-2.5-Pro preferences, creating potential circularity; polishing success is defined by score(C)>score(B) with no margin, a weak and noisy binary metric.
Main results depend heavily on VLM-based judging with an arbitrary score threshold (>=80); although human validation is included, the threshold and evaluator choice are not fully justified.

Some presentation and consistency issues remain: RVPO/VRPO acronym inconsistency, unclear comp_score definition in Algorithm 1, and apparent discrepancies between Table 1 and Table 3 for UI2Code-Real/UI2Code-Synthetic results.

No dedicated limitations section; important limitations such as dependence on VLM evaluators, visual-only optimization versus functional correctness, compute cost, and benchmark contamination risks are not sufficiently discussed.

Novelty is moderate: relative-preference RL and GRPO are existing techniques, and the core contribution is a well-executed application/reformulation; the claimed model-agnostic nature is not empirically validated beyond one model family.
Human evaluation sample sizes are relatively small (80 and 69 tasks) and annotator agreement details are limited, so generalization to broader real-world UI complexity remains partially established.
